analysis.one_liner: Strips the new consumer financial watchdog of its power to ban unfair, deceptive, and abusive practices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in the House or Senate; the consumer bureau kept its authority, and Dodd-Frank remained fully in force.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal Section 1031 of the Dodd-Frank law, the provision that lets the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau prohibit unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts and practices by companies selling financial products to consumers [S2][S3]. That authority is the core tool the bureau uses to police how banks, lenders, and debt collectors treat ordinary customers [S2]. Repealing it would leave the bureau able to enforce narrower rules but unable to go after harmful practices that no specific rule covers [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced by Rep. Connie Mack with three Republican cosponsors and never advanced beyond being referred to subcommittees [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, lenders, credit card issuers, debt collectors, and other companies that sell financial products to consumers would gain if the bill passed. Repealing the bureau's ban on unfair, deceptive, and abusive practices would remove its broadest enforcement tool, leaving them answerable only to specific written rules and reducing the risk of enforcement actions over conduct no rule expressly covers [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 1031 of Dodd-Frank, which authorizes the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to prohibit unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices in connection with any consumer financial product or service.

Also strikes the bureau's related authority to promulgate regulations preventing such practices, and makes conforming changes to Dodd-Frank and the Telemarketing and Consumer Fraud and Abuse Prevention Act.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who use bank accounts, credit cards, mortgages, and other financial products. Without the ban on unfair, deceptive, and abusive practices, the bureau could only act when a company broke a specific written rule, leaving gaps that companies could exploit [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The repeal leaves consumers protected only by rules the bureau happens to have written; harmful or deceptive conduct that falls outside existing rules would no longer be prohibited at all, since the general ban on unfair, deceptive, and abusive practices would no longer exist.

A company facing the bureau's broad authority has a fair argument that Section 1031 gives regulators wide discretion to punish practices no rule clearly forbids, creating legal uncertainty for businesses trying to comply.

Repealing the authority could also narrow the bureau's powers under other consumer laws it inherited from other agencies, because the bill makes conforming changes to how the bureau exercises those inherited powers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers of keeping the authority is the flip side of the bill's cost: Section 1031 was written after the 2008 financial crisis precisely to catch abusive practices that no existing rule anticipated. The strongest case for the bill is regulatory uncertainty for businesses, but that is a trade-off, not a consumer benefit. On balance, repealing this authority would shift risk onto the people who buy financial products.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in House subcommittees after referral and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Connie Mack (R-FL) introduced H.R. 2612 on July 21, 2011, to repeal the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's authority to prohibit unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices.
The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee; three Republicans cosponsored it.

The bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade and the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 112th Congress.
Because the bill never advanced, the consumer bureau retained its authority to prohibit unfair, deceptive, and abusive practices under Dodd-Frank.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers kept the full consumer protection authority the bill would have removed; the finance industry did not get the repeal it sought. Because the bill never became law, no one gained from it — the people who would have been better off under it (finance companies) lost, and ordinary consumers retained existing protections.

for.name: Rep. Connie Mack
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the consumer bureau's ban on unfair, deceptive, and abusive practices.

for.name: Reps. Paul Gosar, Trey Gowdy, and Dennis Ross

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral; never scheduled action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and took no further action; the bill died without a markup or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican, and no Democrat supported the bill; its repeal of a centerpiece of the 2010 Dodd-Frank law drew no recorded Democratic backing [S1][S4].

industries.industry: Consumer finance companies (banks, lenders, credit card issuers, debt collectors)
industries.note: The bill would remove the general prohibition on unfair, deceptive, and abusive practices, leaving these companies subject only to specific written rules and reducing exposure to enforcement over conduct no rule covers. The cost of that freedom falls on the customers the bureau was created to protect.

The bill repeals one of the bureau's core powers, weakening its ability to act against practices not covered by an existing rule. Its interest runs with consumers' interest in keeping the protection in place.
